topic: What is actually a VPN doing? (the tunnel analogy)

beats.narration: Picture your laptop on public Wi-Fi, sending a login request in the clear. The router, your I-S-P, anyone on that network can read exactly where you're going.
That's the baseline. Without protection, every hop between you and the site can see the destination, and often the content too.
A VPN adds a client on your device that encrypts every packet before it ever leaves, router included.

That's the tunnel: an encrypted pipe from you to a VPN server. Your I-S-P still sees traffic leaving your device, but only as opaque bytes headed to the VPN's I-P, not the site you're actually visiting.
At the other end, the VPN server decrypts the packet and forwards your actual request to the real destination, on your behalf.
The response takes the same path in reverse: back to the VPN server, re-encrypted, through your I-S-P, and decrypted only once it reaches your device.
So a VPN tunnel isn't magic. It's encryption between you and a trusted relay, hiding your traffic from the local network. But the VPN provider now sits exactly where your I-S-P used to.
